body.text: But that is not necessarily what middle powers are trying to do. Overall, middle power diplomacy has been less about reshaping the balance of hard power than finding ways to exercise influence within the constraints imposed by it.

Scholars have identified three waves of middle power diplomacy since World War II: first post-war multilateralism, then post-Cold War issue-based activism, and finally the development of less formal groupings such as the G20 and MIKTA after the 2008 global financial crisis. Across these waves, middle powers have sought to establish and promote norms as well as contribute to global governance efforts to tackle common problems.

An emerging debate has pointed to the possibility of a fourth wave of middle power diplomacy since the early 2020s, amid weakening liberal institutions, declining confidence in US support for collective problem-solving, and a growing desire among middle and smaller powers to reduce their dependence on both the United States and China.

While the contours of such diplomacy are still taking shape, a realistic role for middle powers lies not in replacing great power leadership or reorientating power structures but in acting in concert to advance cooperation in specific areas and develop norms for those agendas. This may resemble earlier forms of middle power diplomacy, albeit under different geopolitical conditions.

The protection of critical undersea infrastructure offers an example of what this can look like in practice. Subsea cables and pipelines carry communication, data and energy flows which most states depend on.

At this year’s Shangri-La Dialogue, 17 countries launched the Guiding Principles for Underwater Infrastructure Defence Exchanges (GUIDE), an effort to agree on a common set of principles around undersea infrastructure security and identify practical areas in which defence establishments can cooperate.

Neither China nor the United States were part of this initial agreement. The reasons for their exclusion have not been officially addressed and GUIDE remains open to additional participants. Their absence is nevertheless notable given the wider context in which the initiative emerged, including the aforementioned uncertainty over US leadership in addressing collective challenges, alongside concerns about China’s undersea cable cutting capabilities.

Even without the two great powers, challenges abound. In fact, although there has been broad agreement on the importance of critical undersea infrastructure, its protection has proved difficult for several reasons. Many of these cables lie beyond territorial waters, where responsibility is diffuse and enforcement jurisdiction limited. International law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), offers few tools for holding to account those who interfere with cables.

Vessels that disable their tracking systems or falsify their identity compound the challenges of surveillance and attribution. The problem calls for coordination across governments, agencies and industry. Yet, bringing such a diverse group of stakeholders together will not be an easy task.
